analysis.investment_thesis: Borosil Renewables holds a unique position as India's sole domestic solar glass manufacturer with immense policy tailwinds, but catastrophic margin compression from Chinese dumping has turned it deeply unprofitable (net loss of ₹87 Cr in FY25, EBITDA collapsed 71% from peak ₹256 Cr in FY22). Until anti-dumping duties are enforced and margins structurally recover, this fails Fisher's core test of a superior, self-funding growth business.
key_strengths: India's only domestic solar glass manufacturer — structural monopoly aligned with India's 500 GW renewable target
Completed major capex cycle (₹1,047 Cr over 4 years), creating capacity optionality if margins recover
Diverse product innovation pipeline: anti-reflective, anti-soiling, bifacial, and antimony-free glass variants showing R&D orientation
key_risks: Margin collapse is structural, not cyclical — EBITDA fell from ₹256 Cr (FY22) to ₹73 Cr (FY25) due to Chinese solar glass dumping; no floor yet visible
Revenue growth has decelerated sharply to ~7.7% (FY24→FY25), well below Fisher's 20%+ threshold, with ROE at -8.9% and ROCE at -4.4%
Policy dependency risk — the entire investment thesis hinges on Indian government imposing anti-dumping duties, a regulatory moat rather than an innovation moat Fisher prizes
red_flags: Net profit turned negative and deepening: +₹71 Cr (FY23) → -₹50 Cr (FY24) → -₹87 Cr (FY25)
Free cash flow negative in 4 of last 5 years; operating CF generated only ₹100 Cr in FY25 vs ₹109 Cr capex
Borrowings surged from ₹8 Cr (FY22) to ₹576 Cr (FY24), finance cost up 10x to ₹32 Cr — forced leveraging of a deteriorating business
P/E of 73x is meaningless on negative earnings; actual valuation is severely stretched at 4.7x sales on a loss-making company
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my scuttlebutt method, Borosil Renewables has the makings of a great growth story — a monopoly producer in a structurally expanding market, aligned with India's aggressive solar ambitions. The capacity expansion of over ₹1,000 Cr in capex over four years reflects management's long-term vision. However, the execution has run headlong into Chinese solar glass dumping, which has obliterated any pricing power. EBITDA has fallen from ₹256 Cr in FY22 to just ₹73 Cr in FY25 — a 71% collapse — while revenue only grew modestly to ₹1,476 Cr. Operating income is now just ₹58 Cr on revenues where it once generated ₹223 Cr. This is not a company defending its franchise; it is one that had its margins stripped away by external competition it cannot control.

The critical Fisher test is whether management can maintain or improve margins, and whether the company's moat is real and durable. Here, the moat is entirely regulatory — it exists only if the Indian government enforces anti-dumping protections. That is not the kind of innovation-driven, self-reinforcing competitive advantage I seek. Finance costs have risen 10x to ₹32 Cr as the company borrowed heavily to fund capacity that currently sits underutilized or unprofitably deployed. Debt did fall sharply from ₹576 Cr (FY24) to ₹252 Cr (FY25), suggesting some discipline, but with ongoing losses and negative FCF in 4 of 5 years, capital allocation remains a concern. At 4.7x sales with deeply negative returns, the market is pricing in a full policy-driven recovery that has not yet materialized.
